title: Your favorite discourse
hookLine: of the Majjhima read so far, which one stays

lines: A RAFT, A SAW, A SNAKE.
A HEN, A FIRE, SEVEN CHARIOTS.
cards: About four months ago we opened the Middle-Length Sayings. Since then: a raft, a saw, a snake grabbed by the tail. A hen sitting on her eggs.
A murderer turned monk. A fire that goes out and goes nowhere. Seven chariots in relay.
A potter's roof. Much of it may have blurred, the way books do. But maybe one picture stuck, one you've thought about in the shower, or told a friend.

teach.h: SUTTA: A THREAD TO PICK UP
teach.b: Having a favorite isn't a modern habit. The word for a discourse is sutta, which some readers explain as a thread, the Pali form of the Sanskrit sutra. A thread is something you can pick up again.
And Buddhist communities pick up some threads more than others. In Theravada communities, certain discourses are chanted for protection and blessing.

Some teachers return again and again to a handful, like the one on mindfulness of breathing, or the verse about one fine night: don't chase the past, don't pin hopes on the future. The discourses suggest why.

Remember the day we counted feelings: two, three, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, a hundred and eight. Each count, the Buddha said, was a way of teaching fitted to the listener. Different people needed different doors.

teach.h: A FAVORITE SHOWS WHERE YOU ARE
teach.b: So a favorite isn't a ranking of the teaching. It's a clue to where you are. If the saw stayed with you, maybe you're working with anger.

If it was the raft, maybe with holding on too tight to ideas. The hen on her eggs, maybe with patience. There's a caution too, from the water snake discourse: grab a teaching by the wrong end and it bites.
So ask not only which line you like, but how you're holding it.
And here's a good test of a favorite: read it whole again, setting and questions and all.
Often it says more, or something slightly different, than the version you've been carrying.

how: Many Buddhists return to a few discourses again and again; in Theravada communities some are chanted as paritta for protection and blessing, and some teachers assign students one discourse to study closely for a long time.

practice: Let one picture from these months rise, not the impressive one, the one that comes. Where was it set, who asked the question, what was the image? Sit with it, and notice what it says to you today.

wordCard.voice: Sutta. A thread: the discourse that stayed with you, a clue to where you are, best tested by reading it whole again.

orig.note: Pali sutta, Sanskrit sutra: a discourse. often explained as 'thread', a line of teaching you can pick up again.

carryVoice: Your line: yours. A favorite is a clue to where you stand, not a ranking. See you tomorrow.
